r0.why: Common and widely distributed [1]; high-temperature, high-pressure processes on igneous or sedimentary formations [2]; 2-15 kbar and over 300 C [3]; banded texture [4].

r1.why: Traditional English and North American usage, coarse-grained [7]; grains visible to unaided eye, obvious compositional layers, weak tendency to fracture along them [8]; wider European usage [9].

r2.why: Layers appearing as bands in cross section [19]; gneissic banding [20]; darker bands mafic, more magnesium and iron [21]; lighter bands felsic, feldspar or quartz, lighter elements [22].

r3.why: Banding at high temperature under unequal compression [23]; perpendicular to greatest compression as platy minerals rotate or recrystallize [24]; shearing and deck-of-cards image [25]; stretched like plastic into sheets [26].

r4.why: Sandstone/shale protolith layers metamorphosed to quartzite and mica bands under extreme temperature and pressure [28]; metamorphic differentiation by chemical reactions, not fully understood [29].

r5.why: Many rocks become gneiss so colour and mineral composition are added to names [37]; orthogneiss and paragneiss [16]; augen gneiss from granite with feldspar grains [30]; finer material deforms around them [31].

r6.why: Shields are stable continental cores of exposed ancient rock [38]; gneisses common in their ancient crust [5]; Acasta Gneiss among oldest rocks [6]; gneiss domes in orogenic belts [43].
